summary: Defines HTML 2.0, formalizing the earlier informal specifications of the HyperText Markup Language used for web pages. It was standards-track but is now historic and was replaced by RFC 2854.

plainLanguage.summary: The set of tags web pages use to say this is a heading and this is a link. This is the second version.

subtitle: The language that structures content for web browsers.

tldr.problem: The World Wide Web needed a simple way to structure and present documents with links and multimedia. HTML had evolved through informal practice and needed a formal specification.
tldr.mechanism: HTML 2.0 formalizes the markup language as an application of SGML, defining elements for document structure (headings, paragraphs, lists), hyperlinks, images, and forms, each with specific rendering semantics.
tldr.outcome: HTML 2.0 became the first standardized HTML specification in 1995 but was superseded as HTML evolved with new features and capabilities.

today: RFC 1866 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 2854, which added features like style sheets and scripting. HTML 2.0 is no longer the current standard, but it remains the foundation that all later HTML versions built upon.

sections.title: What is HTML 2.0
sections.content:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is a simple markup language for creating documents that can link to each other and run on any computer. HTML 2.0 is the first formally standardized version, capturing the capabilities of HTML as used on the World Wide Web before June 1994. It was standards-track but is now historic, replaced by RFC 2854.

HTML is based on SGML (Standard Generalized Markup Language), an international standard for describing document structure through markup. Browsers use HTML to understand how to display text, links, images and forms.
sections.plainLanguage: HTML is a set of labels (called 'tags') you put around text to say what it is. 'This is a heading', 'this is a paragraph', 'this is a link'. Version 2.0 is the first official rulebook.

sections.title: Document Structure and Basic Elements
sections.content:
An HTML document has two main parts: the head and the body. The head contains information about the document like the title, which appears in the browser window but not in the main content area. The body contains the visible content: headings, paragraphs, lists, and other elements.

Documents use six heading levels (<H1> through <H6>) to organize content hierarchically, and <P> elements for paragraphs. The specification recommends not skipping heading levels (e.g., jumping from H1 to H3) to preserve document structure. Lists can be unordered (<UL>), ordered (<OL>), or directory-style (<DIR>).
sections.plainLanguage: A web page is like a paper document: the head is like the title page (which you don't see in the actual paper), and the body is the content with headings, paragraphs and lists. You use tags like <P> for a paragraph and <H1> for a big heading.

sections.title: Hyperlinks and Images
sections.content:
Hyperlinks are created with the <A> (anchor) element, which has an HREF attribute pointing to another document's URL. URLs can be absolute (like http://example.com/page.html) or relative (like ../other/page.html). Fragment identifiers (the part after <#>) let you link to a specific named anchor within a document.

The <IMG> element embeds images with a SRC attribute pointing to the image file. Images can be part of a hyperlink (when inside an <A> tag) and can be clickable image maps via the ISMAP attribute, where clicking different regions sends different coordinates to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: A link is made with an <A> tag and the HREF tells where to go when you click it. An image is added with <IMG> and SRC tells where the picture file is.

sections.title: Forms for User Input
sections.content:
Forms collect data from users through input fields, with the <FORM> element wrapping all form fields. The METHOD attribute specifies GET (for searches with no side effects, appending data to the URL) or POST (for operations that modify data, sending data in the request body). The ACTION attribute specifies the URL that processes the form.

Form elements include text input fields (<INPUT TYPE=TEXT>), checkboxes and radio buttons for choices, text areas for multi-line input (<TEXTAREA>), dropdown menus (<SELECT>), and submit/reset buttons. All form data is sent using the application/x-www-form-urlencoded format, where spaces become + and special characters are percent-encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is like a paper questionnaire: you fill in your answers in text boxes, checkboxes and dropdown menus, then click submit to send it. GET is for simple searches, POST is for things that change data.

sections.title: Character Sets and Encoding
sections.content:
HTML 2.0 documents must support the ISO-8859-1 character set (Latin Alphabet No. 1), which includes Western European letters, digits and common symbols. The specification reserves most of this space for future expansion while supporting 191 graphic characters in the current version.

Special characters are represented using entity references like < for <, & for &, and numeric character references like < (ampersand hash 60 semicolon). The specification discourages using tab characters in documents due to inconsistent support, recommending spaces instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers use different letters and symbols. HTML 2.0 mainly uses basic Western European letters. If you need a special character like < or &, you write it as < or & so the browser knows it is not a tag.
